prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that enabled incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 physiology is the strongest case on originality, mechanistic clarity, maturity and breadth of benefit. The chain from proglucagon processing, through identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide and its insulinotropic action, to receptor agonists with glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit has been confirmed by large independent trials and millions of patients. Five of six members ranked it first, which I treat as convergence on the evidence rather than as merit in itself. The Drucker, Holst and Mojsov configuration rests on the academic discovery arc (secretion and physiology, actions and receptor biology, identification of the active peptide), and is what I proposed in my opening ballot.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness. Four names are credited for three slots, and the priority question around identification of the active peptide (Mojsov versus the Habener group) is sensitive and cannot be resolved from the supplied record. Omitting Knudsen leaves out the drug-design step (long-acting acylated analogues) that made the discovery a therapy, so a prize for the physiology alone could be criticised as celebrating the science while skipping the medicine. Habener and other early peptide workers are outside the credited list.

responses.point: Ranked TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) first as a clean bench-to-bedside story with a natural two-person pairing, and proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for GLP-1, replacing Mojsov with Knudsen.
responses.response: I agree the Feldmann-Maini pairing is clean and that the TNF case is mature and overdue, but I ranked it seventh because cytokine-targeted therapy is now a broadly established concept and attribution beyond the pair (Cerami, Beutler, Vilcek, Kollias and others) is incomplete. I disagree on swapping Mojsov for Knudsen. A discovery prize should centre on who identified the active peptide and defined its physiology, and Knudsen's contribution, though clinically decisive, is industrial analogue design that is harder to separate from a company programme. If the committee wants to honour drug development, the better route is a separate part, not displacing the discovery of the active form. I do not see a strong enough reason to lift TNF above CAR-T in my ordering.

responses.point: Placed the unfolded protein response second as a conceptually original organelle-to-nucleus signalling discovery with a compact, well-matched Walter and Mori pairing.
responses.response: I share the view that the UPR is conceptually clean and that Walter and Mori are a tidy pair, which is why I keep it on my list. I ranked it fifth, though, because disease relevance and therapeutic translation are still developing, and the PERK and eIF2 work of Ron and Harding is not in the credited names, so the mammalian branches would be unevenly represented. A UPR prize is defensible as pure cell biology, but I would not rank it above a discovery that has already changed care for very large numbers of patients. It is a sound candidate for a later year or a two-part pairing, not the lead.

responses.point: Ranked optogenetics second and regards a Deisseroth, Nagel, Hegemann trio as a plausible compromise, while stating that leaving out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck is a real fairness problem.
responses.response: I agree with the fairness concern and think it is serious: any three-person optogenetics prize omits at least three credible names, and Miesenböck's earlier genetically targeted photostimulation complicates the priority story. That is part of why I place it third, behind CAR-T, even though I proposed the same trio in my opening ballot. It is also a tool rather than a disease mechanism, which is not disqualifying but makes it a weaker partner for GLP-1 than a medicine-oriented achievement. I think the committee should ask whether the three-person limit makes optogenetics less suitable this year than its scientific merit suggests.

responses.point: Ranked BCR-ABL inhibition and imatinib third as a clean link from molecular lesion to cure-like outcome with a defensible Lydon, Druker and Sawyers trio.
responses.response: I accept that imatinib is the prototype of targeted therapy, that the evidence is very mature, and that I proposed the same trio. My hesitation is attribution and framing: Rowley, Witte, Konopka and others who identified BCR-ABL are not credited, and several of these names have already been recognised together in the Lasker awards, which weakens the sense of an unrecognised achievement. Timing is also late. I rank it sixth and would treat it as a clinical-oncology alternative, not as a competitor to GLP-1. If a second part is wanted, I would prefer CAR-T, whose attribution is broader but whose conceptual novelty is less contested.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can resolve the Mojsov versus Habener priority question about the active GLP-1 peptide from the available evidence.
Whether Knudsen should be credited, either instead of Mojsov or in a separate part, given the weight of drug development in the clinical impact.
Whether a two-part configuration (for example GLP-1 plus CAR-T) improves fairness or merely dilutes a strong single-achievement prize.
For CAR-T, whether Eshhar and others outside the credited names make the June, Sadelain and Rosenberg trio unfair.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén, who are colleagues at Karolinska Institutet, but none of the shortlisted candidates or their work involves those collaborations, and a shared institutional setting is not a recusal issue by itself.
